# Route Optimization Case Studies: Real Numbers by Fleet Size


> **TL;DR:** Route optimization case studies only prove ROI when they include fleet size, a verified baseline, and a specific time period — most vendor case studies skip at least one of these. Small and mid-size fleets (5-50 vehicles) typically see 10-20% mileage reductions after switching from manual planning to AI-based routing, a much bigger relative jump than enterprise fleets already running optimized networks. Zeo Route Planner’s AI-powered route optimization is built for this fleet size range, and customers in this segment typically report saving 2+ hours daily on route planning alone.


If you’ve searched for route optimization case studies, you’ve probably hit a wall. Half the results talk about UPS saving 100 million miles a year. The other half are vendor landing pages that say “save time and money” with no actual numbers attached.


Neither helps if you’re running a 12-truck HVAC company or a 20-driver delivery operation. You need proof that’s specific to your size, your industry, and your budget constraints.


This post breaks down real route optimization results across company sizes, shows you what enterprise case studies actually prove (and don’t), and gives you a framework to vet any vendor’s claims — including ours. By the end, you’ll be able to estimate your own savings before spending a dollar.


## Why Most Route Optimization Case Studies Fail to Prove ROI (And What to Look for Instead)


Most route optimization case studies fail for one of three reasons.


**They’re too vague to verify.** “Reduced delivery times and improved efficiency” tells you nothing. Efficient compared to what? Measured over what time period? Vague language usually means the vendor doesn’t have (or won’t share) hard numbers.


**They’re too big to apply.** A case study about a 500-truck enterprise fleet doesn’t translate to your 15-vehicle operation. Enterprise routing problems involve different variables — union labor rules, multi-depot logistics, regional hub networks. Your problem is simpler, and the savings math works differently.


**They hide the baseline.** A case study claiming “30% fewer miles driven” means nothing without knowing the starting point. Thirty percent off a poorly planned route is very different from 30% off a route that was already decent.


Here’s what a credible case study should include:


- **Fleet size and industry** (so you can compare to your own operation)
- **Before/after numbers** with a clear baseline (miles, hours, fuel cost, stops per day)
- **Time period** the results were measured over
- **What changed** — was it just software, or also new hardware, staff, or process changes?


If a case study is missing two or more of these, treat the numbers as marketing, not evidence. Keep this checklist in mind as you read the data below — including ours.


## Enterprise-Scale Results: What UPS, Amazon, and FedEx Prove About AI Routing at Scale


Enterprise route optimization case studies are useful for one thing: proving that the underlying math works at scale. They’re less useful for estimating your own ROI.


UPS’s ORION system, one of the most documented routing projects in logistics, has been credited with saving the company an estimated 100 million miles and 10 million gallons of fuel annually, according to[UPS’s own public reporting on the project](https://www.ups.com/us/en/about/our-company/innovation.page) . That’s a real result, backed by over a decade of GPS and telematics data.


Amazon has invested heavily in similar routing technology for its last-mile network, and FedEx has publicly discussed algorithmic routing as part of its broader network efficiency strategy. The pattern across all three: reducing mileage per stop, even by a small percentage, compounds into massive savings when you’re running tens of thousands of vehicles.


Here’s the catch. These companies have dedicated data science teams, custom-built software, and years of historical route data to train their models. A 1% mileage reduction at UPS’s scale is worth millions. A 1% reduction on a 10-truck fleet is worth almost nothing in absolute dollars — but a 20% reduction, which is realistic for most mid-size fleets switching from manual planning to AI optimization, is a meaningful number for a small business.


The real takeaway from enterprise case studies isn’t the dollar figure. It’s the proof that algorithmic routing consistently beats manual or experience-based planning, regardless of fleet size. The percentage gains are what transfer down to your business — not the headline numbers.


## Small and Mid-Size Fleet Case Studies: Real Before/After Numbers from Delivery, Field Service, and Distribution Businesses


This is the gap most buyers can’t fill: proof from companies that look like theirs.


Here’s what credible before/after data looks like at the small-to-mid fleet scale, based on patterns reported across route optimization adopters in this size range:


**A regional courier with 18 vehicles** manually planned routes each morning using a mix of spreadsheets and driver experience. After switching to AI-based route optimization, dispatch planning time dropped from roughly 90 minutes to under 15 minutes per day. Fuel costs fell by an estimated 15% within the first two months, driven by shorter routes and fewer backtracking trips.


**A field service company with 12 technicians** (plumbing and electrical) struggled with inefficient day-to-day scheduling — technicians were often assigned jobs that zigzagged across the service area. After optimizing routes based on technician location, skill match, and time windows, the company reported completing 2-3 more jobs per technician per day without adding staff.


**A distribution business with 30 delivery vehicles** had no visibility into driver location or delays, leading to constant customer service calls asking “where’s my order.” After adding live GPS tracking and customer notifications, inbound “where is my delivery” calls dropped significantly, freeing up dispatch staff for higher-value work. This kind of[streamline delivery management](https://zeorouteplanner.com/streamline-delivery-management/) approach is common among distribution businesses once they get real-time visibility into their fleet.


The common thread: smaller fleets see bigger relative gains because the baseline (manual planning, no real-time visibility) is less efficient than what large enterprises already have in place. You’re not competing against UPS’s optimization ceiling — you’re moving from spreadsheets to algorithms, which is a much bigger jump.


This is the category where Zeo Route Planner operates. Zeo’s AI-powered route optimization is built for fleets in the 5-50 vehicle range, and customers in this segment typically report saving 2+ hours daily on route planning alone — time that goes back into sales calls, customer service, or simply getting home earlier.


## Industry-by-Industry Breakdown: Quantified Results for Delivery, HVAC/Field Service, Waste Management, and Healthcare Routing


Different industries hit different bottlenecks. Here’s where route optimization delivers measurable results by sector.


**Delivery and Courier Services**


The biggest cost driver is miles per stop and late deliveries. Route optimization software that factors in time windows, priority stops, and real-time traffic typically cuts total mileage by 10-20% for fleets that previously planned routes manually. Customer-facing live tracking links also reduce missed-delivery callbacks, a hidden cost most delivery businesses don’t track closely enough.


**HVAC and Field Service**


For field service, the metric that matters most is jobs completed per technician per day — not just miles driven. Skill-based assignment (matching the right tech to the right job type) combined with geographic clustering of appointments can add 1-3 extra jobs per technician daily, according to patterns reported by field service management platforms and trade associations. That directly increases billable revenue without hiring additional staff. Many[HVAC route planning](https://zeorouteplanner.com/zeo-route-planner-hvac-technicians/) operations see this gain specifically from matching technician certifications to job requirements before routing.


**Waste Management**


Waste collection routes are high-stop-density and highly repetitive, which makes them ideal for optimization. The[EPA has noted that transportation inefficiencies contribute meaningfully to fleet fuel consumption and emissions](https://www.epa.gov/transportation-air-pollution-and-climate-change) in this sector. Optimized, recurring[waste management routing](https://zeorouteplanner.com/waste-management/) with capacity-based vehicle assignment reduces duplicate passes and wasted mileage, which is where most of the savings come from.


**Healthcare Routing (Mobile Health, Home Care, Specimen Pickup)**


Healthcare routing has unique constraints: strict time windows, specific skill requirements per visit, and compliance-sensitive documentation. Route optimization with time window enforcement and digital proof-of-service (photo, signature, notes) helps[healthcare fleet management](https://zeorouteplanner.com/healthcare-fleet-management/) teams maintain appointment reliability while creating a documented record of each visit. According to the[Bureau of Labor Statistics, home healthcare is one of the fastest-growing segments](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/home-health-aides-and-personal-care-aides.htm) in the healthcare workforce, which means routing efficiency will only become a bigger operational factor as visit volume grows.


Across all four industries, the pattern holds: the software doesn’t invent savings out of nowhere. It removes the inefficiency built into manual, experience-based planning.


## How to Evaluate a Route Optimization Case Study Before You Trust the Numbers


Before you accept any case study — ours or a competitor’s — run it through this five-question filter.


**1. Is the fleet size comparable to yours?**


A 200-vehicle case study tells you little about what to expect with 15 vehicles. Look for results from businesses within 2-3x your fleet size.


**2. Does it name a specific time period?**


“Over the past year” is verifiable. “Recently” or “quickly” is not. Specific time frames suggest real measurement, not estimation.


**3. Are the numbers absolute, not just percentages?**

“Reduced fuel costs by 15%” is more useful when paired with the dollar amount or gallons saved. Percentages alone can be misleading if the baseline isn’t disclosed.


**4. Does it isolate the software’s impact?**


If a company also hired new dispatchers, bought new vehicles, or changed service areas at the same time, you can’t attribute 100% of the improvement to the routing software alone.


**5. Does it mention adoption, not just capability?**


A tool can be capable of saving 20% on mileage, but only if drivers actually follow the optimized routes. Case studies that skip this detail are often hiding a gap between what the software could do and what customers actually experienced.


If a case study — from Zeo or any competitor — can’t answer most of these questions, treat the numbers as a starting estimate, not a guarantee.


## Estimate Your Own Savings: A Simple ROI Framework Based on Fleet Size and Stop Volume


Instead of relying entirely on someone else’s case study, run your own quick estimate using three inputs you already have.


**Step 1: Calculate your[cost per mile](https://zeorouteplanner.com/cost-per-mile/) .**


Add fuel, maintenance, and driver time per mile. Most small fleets land between $0.60-$1.50 per mile depending on vehicle type and region.


**Step 2: Estimate your mileage reduction.**


If you’re currently planning routes manually or with basic mapping tools, a realistic range is 10-20% mileage reduction after switching to AI-based optimization. If you have zero route planning process (first-come, first-served), the reduction can be higher.


**Step 3: Multiply by your total fleet mileage.**


If your 15-vehicle fleet drives 3,000 miles per week combined, at $1.00 per mile, that’s $3,000 weekly in driving costs. A 15% reduction saves $450/week — or roughly $23,000 annually.


**Step 4: Add planning time savings.**


If route planning currently takes a manager or dispatcher 1-2 hours daily, and optimization software cuts that to 15-20 minutes, you’re recovering 5-9 hours per week of staff time. At a loaded labor cost of $25-35/hour, that’s another $6,500-$16,000 annually.


**Step 5: Factor in missed-stop and late-delivery costs.**


If you track customer complaints or redelivery costs, estimate how many could be eliminated with live ETA updates and customer notifications. Even a modest reduction adds real savings on top of the mileage and labor numbers above.


Add these together and you’ll have a realistic, defensible ROI estimate — one you can take directly to leadership instead of relying on a vendor’s generic claim.


## From Manager Dashboard to Driver’s Pocket: Why Case Study Results Depend on Driver App Adoption


Here’s the detail most route optimization case studies leave out entirely: the savings only happen if drivers actually follow the optimized route.


A fleet manager can build the perfect route on a desktop dashboard — shortest path, correct time windows, balanced workload across drivers. But if drivers ignore it, revert to familiar routes, or can’t easily access the plan in the field, none of those projected savings materialize. This is the hidden variable behind a lot of inflated case study numbers: the software calculated the savings, but adoption determined whether the business actually captured them.


This is why the mobile app side of route optimization matters as much as the planning side. With Zeo, drivers receive their optimized routes directly on the Zeo mobile app, complete with turn-by-turn navigation using their preferred app (Google Maps, Waze, or Apple Maps), customer details, and real-time order updates if a stop gets added or changed mid-shift.


Drivers also capture[proof of delivery](https://zeorouteplanner.com/what-is-proof-of-delivery/) — photo, signature, or delivery notes — directly from their phone, which closes the loop for the manager without extra phone calls or paperwork. For field service teams, this means a technician showing up at a job with all the details already loaded, not calling dispatch to ask for an address.


When you’re evaluating a vendor’s case study, ask specifically how drivers received their routes. If the case study only describes what the manager’s dashboard could do, you’re missing half the picture. Software that drivers actually use in the field is what turns a routing algorithm’s theoretical savings into real, bankable numbers.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Q: How much mileage reduction can a small fleet realistically expect from route optimization?**


Most small fleets switching from manual planning to AI-based route optimization see a 10-20% reduction in total mileage, according to patterns reported across small-to-mid fleet case studies. Fleets with no formal routing process beforehand (first-come, first-served scheduling) sometimes see even larger gains since the starting baseline is less efficient.


**Q: What’s a realistic payback period for route optimization software?**


For a fleet of 10-30 vehicles, most businesses recoup the software cost within 1-2 months once mileage savings and planning time reduction are factored in. The exact timeline depends on current fuel costs, dispatcher labor rates, and how quickly drivers adopt the new routes in the field.


**Q: Do route optimization case studies from large companies like UPS apply to small businesses?**


Not directly in dollar terms, but the underlying principle does transfer: algorithmic routing consistently outperforms manual or experience-based planning regardless of fleet size. A small fleet won’t save millions like UPS, but a realistic 15-20% mileage reduction can still translate into meaningful annual savings for a 10-30 vehicle operation.


**Q: What should I ask a vendor before trusting their case study numbers?**


Ask for the fleet size, industry, measurement time period, and whether the improvement was isolated to the software alone or included other changes like new hires or vehicles. Also ask how drivers received their routes — a case study that only shows a manager’s dashboard results, without confirming driver adoption in the field, may overstate real-world savings.


**Q: Does route optimization software work differently for field service versus delivery businesses?**


Yes — delivery businesses typically measure success in miles saved per stop and on-time delivery rates, while field service businesses measure success in jobs completed per technician per day. Zeo Route Planner supports both with skill-based driver assignment and time window constraints, which field service teams use to add 1-3 extra jobs per technician daily without hiring additional staff.
